svg.title: Acid into bases: read the direction and count protons
svg.desc: A four-panel teaching figure gives downward pH curves for hydrochloric acid added to ammonia and to sodium carbonate, with the titrant direction explicit. Ammonia half-equivalence at12.5 mL gives conjugate-acid pKa9.25 and equivalence25 mL is acidic. Carbonate equivalences12.5/25 mL correspond to bicarbonate and carbon-dioxide-containing forms; stoichiometry, approximate model pH values and mid-buffer points are labelled. The carbonate curve is explicitly a CO2-retaining dilute equilibrium model; gas loss in an open flask can change measured pH.

g.text: Acid into bases: read the direction and count protons
Ammonia has one protonation step; carbonate has two. Curves are calculated from mass and charge balance.
Ammonia: acid goes into the base
pH
HCl added / mL
Model: 25.0 mL of 0.100 M NH₃; add 0.100 M HCl at 25 °C.
pKₐ(NH₄⁺) = 9.25. The curve falls because acid is the titrant.
Name the pair before reading pKₐ
① Half-equivalence: 12.5 mL
NH₃ and NH₄⁺ form a buffer.
pH ≈ pKₐ(NH₄⁺) = 9.25.
② Equivalence: 25.0 mL
NH₄⁺ is the principal nitrogen species.
It donates H⁺ to water: pH ≈ 5.28.
NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
The half-equivalence rule uses pKₐ of NH₄⁺, not pKᵦ of NH₃.
After equivalence, excess strong acid controls pH.
Carbonate: two protonation steps
pH
HCl added / mL
Model: 20.0 mL of 0.0750 M Na₂CO₃; add 0.120 M HCl. pKₐ
values 6.35 and 10.33; 25 °C; dissolved CO₂ is retained.
Count total acid, not just the last step
① First equivalence: 12.5 mL
CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ → HCO₃⁻
Main form: HCO₃⁻; pH ≈ 8.34.
② Second equivalence: 25.0 mL
HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → CO₂(aq) + H₂O
Two H⁺ per initial CO₃²⁻; pH ≈ 3.91.
Buffer midpoints: 6.25 mL → pH ≈ 10.33;
CO₂(aq) includes its hydrated acid form in this model. An open
flask loses CO₂, so real pH values can differ; the 1:1 and 2:1
acid counts remain.
MARLBRIDGE • Calculated curves; model conditions stated in each panel.
